title: What drives our behaviors in buildings? A review on occupant interactions with building systems from the lens of behavioral theories
central_proposition: This paper reviews and synthesizes how psychological, sociological, and economic behavioral theories have been applied to explain occupant interactions with various building systems, identifying common theories, methodologies, findings, and research gaps.

concept_definitions.name: Behavior
concept_definitions.definition: represents whether or the extent to which one typically practices a given behavior.

concept_definitions.name: Behavioral intention
concept_definitions.definition: represents the extent to which an individual intends or plans to practice a given behavior within a given time frame and context.

concept_definitions.name: Attitudes
concept_definitions.definition: reflect an individual's beliefs about likely positive and negative consequences of performing a particular behavior.

concept_definitions.name: Subjective norms (social norms)
concept_definitions.definition: individuals' beliefs about the extent to which important others expect them to engage in the behavior.

concept_definitions.name: Perceived behavioral control
concept_definitions.definition: individuals' beliefs about their ability to enact the behavior (capacity) and whether or not their actions are completely under their control (autonomy).

concept_definitions.name: Norms (Energy Cultures Framework)
concept_definitions.definition: represent shared beliefs on how individuals should behave in a given context, expectations and/or aspirations about what we do and what we have.

concept_definitions.name: Material culture (Energy Cultures Framework)
concept_definitions.definition: represents the technologies and infrastructures that influence the use of energy, both functional and symbolic.

argument_structure: The paper systematically reviews existing literature by first outlining its methodology and selection criteria. It then provides an overview of identified behavioral theories and their core constructs. The main body synthesizes the application of these theories to occupant interactions with specific building systems (HVAC, windows, lighting/shading, electronic devices, domestic hot water, and mixed systems), detailing methodologies, applied theories, general findings, and research gaps for each. Finally, it discusses general shortcomings and provides directions for future research.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The paper synthesizes the causal mechanisms proposed by various psychological, sociological, and economic theories, which generally posit that individual and collective behaviors are driven by factors such as attitudes, beliefs, norms, perceived control, motivations, and social practices, influencing interactions with building systems and energy consumption.

findings.consequent: Intentions to save energy related to home heating
findings.mechanism: Attitudes reflect beliefs about consequences, and subjective norms reflect perceived social expectations, both shaping intentions to act.
findings.quote: energy-saving attitudes and subjective norm beliefs were significant predictors of intentions to save energy related to home heating

findings.antecedent: Intentions to save energy related to home heating
findings.consequent: Heat-use habits, Purchase of energy-saving products for home heating
findings.mechanism: Stronger intentions translate into actual behaviors and purchasing decisions.
findings.quote: those intentions had a positive influence on heat-use habits and the purchase of energy-saving products for home heating.

findings.antecedent: Perceived behavioral control, Descriptive norms beliefs
findings.consequent: Intentions or behaviors related to saving energy for heating
findings.mechanism: In this context, individuals' perceived ability to perform the behavior or their perception of what others do did not significantly influence their intentions or actions.
findings.quote: neither perceived behavioral control nor descriptive norms beliefs predicted intentions or behaviors related to saving energy for heating.

findings.mechanism: External incentives (rewards) can motivate behavioral change by altering the perceived costs/benefits of an action.
findings.quote: playing the game to earn points and rewards lead to reduced use of air-conditioning

findings.antecedent: Interventions addressing occupants' motivations, moral norms, perceived behavioral control (self-efficacy)
findings.mechanism: Activating personal norms (sense of moral obligation) and enhancing self-efficacy can motivate individuals to engage in pro-environmental behaviors.
findings.quote: interventions addressing occupants' motivations, moral norms, and perceived behavioral control (or self-efficacy) to save energy can somewhat reduce heat energy use

findings.antecedent: Attitudes toward saving energy (money, thermal comfort, environment, social motivations)
findings.mechanism: Individual beliefs and evaluations of the outcomes of saving energy (financial, comfort, environmental, social) influence how they interact with HVAC systems.
findings.quote: attitudes toward saving energy in order to save money... attitudes related to thermal comfort... attitudes toward saving energy to protect the environment... and attitudes toward saving energy for social motivations predicted system interactions.

findings.mechanism: Values reflecting concern for the environment can drive pro-environmental behaviors.
findings.quote: stronger biospheric values were found to reduce the use of heating

findings.mechanism: Values reflecting self-interest can lead to behaviors that prioritize personal comfort or cost savings over energy conservation.
findings.quote: stronger egoistic values were found to increase heating use.

findings.mechanism: The influence of these values on heating behavior is complex and can vary depending on context or individual interpretation.
findings.quote: Altruistic and hedonic values had mixed effects on heating use.

findings.antecedent: Feedback on energy use related to heating or cooling
findings.mechanism: Simple feedback alone may not be sufficient to motivate behavioral change without additional interventions or motivational factors.
findings.quote: providing users with feedback on energy use related to heating or cooling did not influence subsequent use.

findings.antecedent: Residents' 'energy literacy' (knowledge of heating system functionality), Difficulty of regulating systems, Perceptions of comfortable temperatures
findings.consequent: Own regulation of thermostats and room temperatures
findings.mechanism: Knowledge, perceived ease of use, and comfort expectations influence how individuals interact with and control their heating systems.
findings.quote: residents attributed 'energy literacy'... the difficulty of regulating their systems, and their perceptions of comfortable temperatures to their own regulation of thermostats and room temperatures.

findings.antecedent: Moral norms, Feedback on energy use
findings.mechanism: In some contexts, a sense of moral obligation or simple feedback may not be strong enough drivers for HVAC-related energy saving behaviors.
findings.quote: moral norms... and feedback... found not to have an influence on interaction with HVAC-related systems

findings.antecedent: Feedback about relative performance (leading to competition, social comparison, social pressure)
findings.mechanism: Social comparison and competitive feedback can motivate individuals to align their behavior with perceived social norms or desired outcomes.
findings.quote: feedback about relative performance leading to the feeling of competition, social comparison, or social pressure is effective in promoting pro-environmental behavior.

findings.mechanism: Interventions can induce habit formation or sustained changes in behavioral intentions.
findings.quote: even short treatments have a lasting effect of several weeks on occupant behavior.

findings.mechanism: Behaviors are embedded within broader social and cultural contexts, making individual preferences less influential than collective norms.
findings.quote: ventilation behaviors are part of 'culturally recognized social practices' (p. 521) individual preferences play a minor role.

findings.consequent: Ventilation behavior in summer and winter
findings.mechanism: Cognitive factors (knowledge, perceptions) and affective states (satisfaction) influence how individuals decide to ventilate.
findings.quote: Ventilation behavior in summer and winter can be explained by factors such as knowledge, perceptions, and satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Interventions based on modified Norm Activation Model
findings.consequent: Observed and self-reported closed windows in winter
findings.mechanism: Activating personal norms and awareness of consequences can motivate individuals to close windows for energy saving.
findings.quote: a significant increase in observed and self-reported closed windows in winter can be achieved by interventions based on their modified Norm Activation Model.

findings.antecedent: Pot plants preventing full opening of windows, Perceived efficiency, effectiveness, and economic efficiency of trickle ventilation, Participants' strong affinity (attitudes) for pot plants
findings.consequent: Behavior of trickle ventilation, Heating energy use
findings.mechanism: Material objects (pot plants) and subjective perceptions (efficiency, attitudes) interact within social practices to influence ventilation and energy use.
findings.quote: behavior of trickle ventilation... with objectively observable aspects, such as pot plants preventing the full opening of windows together with subjective aspects.

findings.antecedent: Mismatch between materiality (newly refurbished apartments) and practice (former heating and ventilation behavior), Meanings (need for fresh air), Competences (knowledge of ventilation strategies)
findings.mechanism: Discrepancies between the physical environment, established routines, and cognitive frameworks (meanings, competences) influence how occupants adapt to new building systems.
findings.quote: mismatch between materiality... and practice... in combination with meanings... competences

findings.antecedent: Building-related influences (mechanical ventilation with heat recovery, demographics)
findings.mechanism: Building features and occupant characteristics interact to shape ventilation behaviors.
findings.quote: building-related influences such as the existence of mechanical ventilation with heat recovery and demographics have an influence on the frequency of opening windows

findings.antecedent: Energy efficiency of the building envelope
findings.mechanism: The physical efficiency of the building envelope does not directly translate to occupant ventilation behavior, suggesting other factors are more dominant.
findings.quote: the energy efficiency of the building envelope is not correlated.

findings.mechanism: Physiological and comfort needs are primary motivators for engaging in ventilation behaviors.
findings.quote: motivational drivers for window opening is frequently driven by the need for fresh air

findings.antecedent: Indoor or outdoor temperature (too hot or cold), Noise levels
findings.mechanism: Environmental conditions (temperature, noise) directly influence comfort and drive behaviors to mitigate discomfort.
findings.quote: for window closing is driven by the indoor or outdoor temperature (e.g., too hot or cold) as well as to reduce the noise levels.

findings.mechanism: Individual psychological characteristics provide additional explanatory power beyond environmental factors in predicting behavior.
findings.quote: prediction of the window opening is improved when adding psychological elements such as personality traits or self-efficacy

findings.antecedent: Lack of knowledge of AC inefficiency, Environmental values
findings.consequent: Not opening windows when AC is cooling
findings.mechanism: A lack of understanding of energy implications, combined with environmental values, can lead to behaviors that are not energy-efficient.
findings.quote: high percentage (69%) of respondents who reported to never open the window when the air-conditioning is cooling the room with environmental values based on lack of knowledge of the inefficiency

findings.consequent: Pro-environmental behaviors in relation to lighting
findings.mechanism: The framework of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control can effectively model intentions and behaviors for lighting.
findings.quote: TPB can fit the data well in order to explain pro-environmental behaviors in relation to lighting.

findings.mechanism: Automatic, routinized behaviors (habits) can be more influential than conscious intentions in predicting actions.
findings.quote: habit was a stronger predictor of light switching behaviors, in comparison to intentions.

findings.mechanism: Social influences and established routines are key drivers of intentions related to lighting behavior.
findings.quote: social-cognitive factors and habits were mostly significant predictors of intention

findings.mechanism: When social expectations are salient, individuals' perceptions of what is normal or expected become more influential.
findings.quote: when relevant social norms are salient, perceived norms play a more prominent role.

findings.mechanism: For simple, routine behaviors, the feeling of control over one's actions may not be a strong motivator.
findings.quote: Perceived autonomy also did not heavily influence simple, daily energy-saving behaviors.

findings.antecedent: Number of people sharing a space
findings.consequent: Inclination to switch lights off when no one is present
findings.mechanism: Shared responsibility in a group setting can diffuse individual accountability, leading to less pro-environmental behavior.
findings.quote: number of people sharing a space, the less inclined one is to switch lights off when no one is present, suggesting that shared responsibility... may be affected by other occupants' presence

findings.mechanism: The extended TPB model may not capture all contextual factors influencing behavior in different organizational settings.
findings.quote: extended TPB model did not fully account for organizational differences in light switching behaviors

findings.mechanism: Blinds can mitigate solar gain in hot climates, improving both energy efficiency and thermal comfort.
findings.quote: in a hot climate, blinds are effective for energy performance and comfort.

findings.consequent: Effective control of comfort and energy performance
findings.mechanism: In hot climates, managing radiant heat gain is more critical for comfort and energy than air movement.
findings.quote: in a hot climate, solar radiation was more important than air movement for effective control of both comfort and energy performance.

findings.consequent: Effective control of comfort and energy performance
findings.mechanism: In cold climates, controlling drafts and air infiltration is more critical for comfort and energy than managing solar radiation.
findings.quote: for a cold climate, the controlling of air movement became more effective than controlling solar radiation.

findings.mechanism: Higher motivation drives individuals to engage in actions that conserve energy.
findings.quote: motivation level of occupants can affect energy-saving behaviors.

findings.antecedent: Occupancy interventions (thermal comfort, peer-pressure, improving self-assessed knowledge of energy conservation)
findings.consequent: Occupants' motivation level, Energy-saving lighting and shading interactions
findings.mechanism: Interventions that address comfort, social influence, and knowledge can enhance motivation and lead to energy-saving behaviors.
findings.quote: occupancy interventions can be utilized to (1) provide thermal comfort conditions for occupants, (2) utilize peer-pressure among coworkers, and (3) promote their motivation level of occupants by improving self-assessed knowledge of occupants on energy conservation.

findings.antecedent: Distributing information about energy consumption facts and reduction guidelines
findings.mechanism: Passive information dissemination alone may not be sufficient to change behavior without active engagement or motivational strategies.
findings.quote: distributing information about energy consumption facts and reduction guidelines is not effective in influencing occupants.

findings.consequent: Promoting energy conservation behaviors among occupants
findings.mechanism: Active feedback and social comparison provide salient information and social pressure that can effectively motivate behavioral change.
findings.quote: feedback and peer-comparison are among the most effective education methods on promoting energy conservation behaviors among the occupants.

findings.antecedent: Knowledge of environmental risks, Awareness of consequences
findings.mechanism: Knowledge and awareness alone are not sufficient to drive widespread energy-saving behavior; other factors like intrinsic motivation or economic consequences are also important.
findings.quote: despite their knowledge of environmental risks and awareness of consequences, only a small group of the participants demonstrated energy-saving behaviors.

findings.mechanism: Without external incentives or disincentives, individuals may not be motivated to change energy-intensive behaviors.
findings.quote: lack of economic consequences (extrinsic motives) has contributed to excessive energy consumption behavior.

findings.mechanism: Raising awareness and engaging the public through educational initiatives can foster a culture of energy conservation.
findings.quote: education, public engagement, and awareness are the best options for domestic energy conservation in Qatar.

findings.antecedent: Hedonic goals, Normative goals (from Goal Framing Theory)
findings.consequent: Lighting interaction behaviors (e.g., purchase of energy-efficient lamps)
findings.mechanism: Goals related to pleasure/comfort (hedonic) and social appropriateness/responsibility (normative) frame how individuals make decisions about lighting.
findings.quote: two types of goals from the Goal Framing Theory (hedonic and normative goals) can guide certain lighting interaction behaviors in single-family houses, such as the purchase of energy-efficient lamps.

findings.antecedent: Changes in lighting purchase behavior (use of energy-efficient lamp technology)
findings.mechanism: Adopting new technology does not automatically translate to changes in daily habits; the two behaviors may be driven by different factors.
findings.quote: Changes in lighting purchase behavior... did not significantly correlate with changes in lighting interaction habits.

findings.antecedent: Energy saving related to lighting behavior
findings.consequent: Prevalent among participants, Achievable without serious intervention
findings.mechanism: Some energy-saving behaviors are already common practice and do not require strong external motivators.
findings.quote: energy saving related to lighting behavior is already prevalent among the participants and achievable even without serious intervention and campaigning

findings.antecedent: Energy-saving lighting habits (e.g., turning off lights upon departure)
findings.mechanism: Established routines contribute to overall energy conservation.
findings.quote: prevalence of energy-saving lighting habits, such as turning off the lights upon departure (as the last person) [32,79].

findings.mechanism: Targeted interventions can successfully modify occupant behaviors related to lighting and shading.
findings.quote: evidence also supported the effectiveness of interventions on lighting and shading interactions [32,96].

findings.consequent: Variance in PC switching off intentions
findings.mechanism: Attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control are strong predictors of intentions to switch off computers.
findings.quote: TPB constructs were able to explain 61% of the variance in PC switching off intentions

findings.mechanism: Routinized behaviors (habits) directly influence energy consumption, even for specific devices.
findings.quote: habit construct... was the only one being significantly associated with energy consumption, explaining about 11% of the variance

findings.consequent: Self-reported energy-saving behaviors (printing smaller, not printing emails, switching off monitors, switching off lights)
findings.mechanism: Combining conscious intentions (TPB) with automatic routines (habit) provides a comprehensive model for predicting various energy-saving behaviors.
findings.quote: A similar research model (TPB plus habit) has been applied by Lo et al. [32], analyzing its predictive power regarding self-reported energy-saving behaviors

findings.antecedent: Social Practice Theory (applied to university research group setting)
findings.mechanism: Social practices, including collective norms and shared meanings, can lead to greater energy consumption increases (rebound effect) than individual-level factors alone.
findings.quote: much higher rebound effects were identified than compared to an individual-oriented perspective.

findings.antecedent: Specialization of ITC-branches ('bulge'), Availability of data analysis services ('more is never enough')
findings.mechanism: Organizational structures and perceived unlimited access to resources can drive increased energy consumption.
findings.quote: main drivers for this development, specialization of ITC-branches... and the availability of data analysis services... were identified.

findings.mechanism: SPT shifts focus from income to built environment, household practices, and appliance characteristics as drivers of consumption.
findings.quote: SPT helped to identify and shift the focus on non-income factors that influence appliance ownership and ultimately electricity consumption

findings.mechanism: Sustained feedback can lead to gradual behavioral adjustments over time.
findings.quote: A reduction of energy usage could be observed during the later stage of the monitoring phase

findings.antecedent: Individual variables (values regarding biosphere, attitude towards technology)
findings.mechanism: In this context, broad individual values and attitudes did not directly translate to measurable energy reduction.
findings.quote: no significant associations of individual variables (values regarding biosphere, attitude towards technology) and energy reduction were found.

findings.antecedent: Intervention based on Norm Activation Model
findings.mechanism: Activating personal norms and awareness of consequences can lead to significant energy savings.
findings.quote: energy savings observed amounted to 43% (electricity) and 10% (heating) of the calculated maximum saving potential.

findings.mechanism: Modifying established routines is key to achieving sustained energy conservation.
findings.quote: habit changes are the drivers of energy-saving efforts.

findings.antecedent: Education on climate-relevant issues (Social Cognitive Theory)
findings.consequent: Conservation behavior index (hang drying clothes, switching off appliances)
findings.mechanism: Providing knowledge and fostering self-efficacy through education can lead to behavioral changes.
findings.quote: index measuring conservation behavior increased by 26.5% based on self-report, with the greatest changes occurring in hang drying clothes as well as switching off appliances.

findings.mechanism: Social recognition and approval can be more powerful motivators for energy conservation than financial incentives.
findings.quote: social rewards generally had a stronger positive effect on energy conservation than the monetary rewards

findings.mechanism: Public visibility of feedback enhances social comparison and accountability, leading to greater behavioral change.
findings.quote: public feedback had a stronger effect than feedback provided privately.

findings.mechanism: Monetary incentives can sometimes backfire, leading to a reduction in intrinsic motivation or a perception that the behavior is only for reward.
findings.quote: private monetary rewards were shown to be counter-productively, leading to an increase in electricity consumption of 3.2%.

findings.antecedent: Social reward conditions (after cessation of rewarding)
findings.mechanism: Socially motivated behavioral changes can be more internalized and sustained even after external incentives are removed.
findings.quote: eight weeks after cessation of rewarding, people in the social reward conditions were still conserving energy, showing the enduring effect of this intervention.

findings.antecedent: Intervention designed according to Construal Level Theory
findings.mechanism: Aligning interventions with the psychological distance of the behavior can enhance effectiveness.
findings.quote: intervention designed according to Construal Level Theory helped all experimental groups reduce water use over a six-week period.

findings.antecedent: Interventions aligned with their level of construal
findings.mechanism: Interventions are more effective when they match the abstractness or concreteness with which individuals perceive the behavior.
findings.quote: interventions which align their level of construal were marginally more effective at reducing water use than those that did not.

findings.antecedent: Four typologies of hot water use in residential sector
findings.consequent: Residents' ways of interacting with hot water systems
findings.mechanism: Different behavioral patterns exist, suggesting that interventions need to be tailored to specific user groups.
findings.quote: four typologies of hot water use in the residential sector, suggesting residents have distinctly different ways of interacting with their hot water systems.

findings.antecedent: Psychological constructs (attitudes, subjective norm, perceived behavior control)
findings.mechanism: Aggregate psychological factors can be more predictive of household-level consumption than individual-focused theoretical constructs.
findings.quote: psychological constructs such as attitudes, subjective norm, and perceived behavior control can be more useful in predicting household-level water consumption

findings.antecedent: Sociodemographic, psychosocial, behavioral, and infrastructure variables
findings.mechanism: A combination of individual, social, and environmental factors collectively influences household water consumption.
findings.quote: sociodemographic, psychosocial, behavioral and infrastructure variables play a significant role in determining household water use.

findings.mechanism: An individual's moral obligation to save energy influences their showering duration.
findings.quote: personal norms explained 5% of the variance in occupant time spent showering

findings.consequent: Intentions to save energy (domestic hot water)
findings.mechanism: An individual's moral obligation to save energy strongly influences their intentions to do so for domestic hot water.
findings.quote: personal norms explained... 18% of the variance in intentions to save energy.

findings.mechanism: These psychological factors collectively influence individuals' willingness and ability to engage in energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: large majority supported the positive impact of attitudes, norms, and perceived control on the performance of energy conservation behaviors in buildings.

findings.consequent: Intentions towards energy savings, Self-reported energy-saving behaviors (at home and work)
findings.mechanism: Positive attitudes foster intentions and actual engagement in energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: individuals' attitudes towards energy conservation have been found to positively influence intentions towards energy savings... in addition to self-reported energy-saving behaviors at home and at work

findings.mechanism: A belief in one's ability to perform a behavior (perceived control) increases the likelihood of intending and performing that behavior.
findings.quote: occupants' perceived control positively influenced both intentions and behaviors around energy conservation

findings.antecedent: Subjective norms, Personal norms, Peer pressure
findings.consequent: Intention to undertake, Actually perform energy conservation behaviors
findings.mechanism: Social expectations, moral obligations, and peer influence motivate individuals to engage in energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: Subjective norms... personal norms... and peer pressure... were shown to positively influence intention to undertake and actually perform energy conservation behaviors.

findings.mechanism: Norms related to environmental responsibility and perceptions of what others do can motivate pro-environmental choices.
findings.quote: environmental-personal norms and descriptive norms were also identified through self-reported surveys evaluating energy-conservation behaviors and intentions as a motivating factor for people to move to green buildings

findings.antecedent: Descriptive norms, Organizational energy-saving climate, Media publicity (stimulus)
findings.consequent: Employee's perceived energy-saving responsibility, Social pressure (organism), Energy saving intentions (response)
findings.mechanism: Social cues, organizational culture, and media influence perceptions of responsibility and social pressure, which in turn shape intentions.
findings.quote: descriptive norms, organizational energy-saving climate, and media publicity... had a significant direct and positive impact on employee's perceived energy-saving responsibility and social pressure... and consequently on energy saving intentions

findings.mechanism: In some contexts, attitudes alone may not be sufficient to drive actual energy conservation behavior.
findings.quote: reported no significant effect of attitudes on energy conservation behavior

findings.mechanism: The influence of social and personal norms can vary and may not be significant in all contexts for energy conservation.
findings.quote: Gao et al. [46] and Hewitt et al. [62] showed insignificant effects of social and personal norms on energy conservation behaviors, respectively.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Gao et al. [46], Hewitt et al. [62]

findings.consequent: Energy conservation (switching off appliances and other devices)
findings.mechanism: Belief in one's ability to perform a behavior (self-efficacy) directly promotes energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: self-efficacy... can result in a positive influence on energy conservation, specifically for switching off appliances and other devices.

findings.antecedent: Opportunities to control building and individual systems
findings.consequent: Saving energy, Office productivity, Thermal comfort
findings.mechanism: The impact of control opportunities is complex and can have varied outcomes across different performance metrics.
findings.quote: opportunities to control building and individual systems were shown to have mixed impacts on saving energy, office productivity, and thermal comfort

findings.mechanism: Providing individuals with direct control over their environment can empower them to make energy-saving choices.
findings.quote: individual control systems can facilitate energy saving behavior.

findings.mechanism: Values that prioritize the well-being of others and the environment drive pro-environmental behaviors.
findings.quote: self-transcendence and biospheric values have a positive influence on energy savings

findings.mechanism: Understanding the negative impacts of energy consumption can motivate individuals to conserve energy.
findings.quote: awareness of consequences on energy conservation behaviors and intentions [43,155].

findings.mechanism: In some contexts, simply being aware of consequences may not be a strong enough motivator for behavioral change.
findings.quote: van der Werff and Steg [56] did not find awareness of consequences having a significant effect on energy conservation behavior.

findings.mechanism: Beliefs about the severity of climate change can influence individuals' energy consumption patterns.
findings.quote: Huebner et al. [160] found a positive relationship between beliefs about climate change and energy consumption

findings.mechanism: General beliefs may not directly translate into specific energy-saving practices without other mediating factors.
findings.quote: no significant effect was found between beliefs and energy-saving practices [161].

findings.mechanism: Anticipating negative emotions may not be a primary driver for forming energy-saving intentions.
findings.quote: negatively anticipated emotions were not significantly related to intentions

findings.mechanism: Anticipating positive feelings from energy-saving actions can motivate individuals to form intentions.
findings.quote: positively anticipated emotions were significant predictors of them.

findings.consequent: Satisfaction with environmental comfort, Energy saving behavior
findings.mechanism: Intentions to save energy can result in both increased comfort satisfaction and actual energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: energy saving intentions lead to higher satisfaction with environmental comfort and energy saving behavior.

findings.consequent: Intent to save energy at work
findings.mechanism: The specific reasons for acting and the underlying functions of attitudes shape intentions for energy saving in the workplace.
findings.quote: different motivations and attitude functions determine intent to save energy at work.

findings.consequent: Heating and cooling related behaviors, Energy consumption
findings.mechanism: The influence of these motivations is complex and can vary depending on context and individual factors.
findings.quote: mixed results around the role of financial, environmental, and social motivations to impact heating and cooling related behaviors and energy consumption.

findings.antecedent: Bill consciousness, Needs for warmness and coolness, Sense of community, Perceived usefulness, Percentage of risk of analyzed device, Socio-demographic variables (income, household size, age, gender, climate zone), Number of children, Occupants' education level
findings.consequent: Energy conservation intentions and behaviors, Energy use
findings.mechanism: A wide range of individual, social, and contextual factors beyond core psychological constructs contribute to energy-related behaviors.
findings.quote: bill consciousness and needs for warmness and coolness [48], sense of community [44], perceived usefulness and percentage of risk of the analyzed device [50], socio-demographic variables such as income, household size, age, gender, and climate zone [42,48,58], and the number of children in a household and occupants' education level [47]

findings.mechanism: Positive attitudes within a household can lead to energy-saving behaviors.
findings.quote: household energy saving attitudes can impact energy conservation and heating use.

findings.mechanism: Established routines and habits strongly dictate daily energy-related behaviors.
findings.quote: occupant behavior in Spanish household was followed a very constant daily routine and habit patterns.

findings.antecedent: Feedback combined with goal setting, peer education
findings.mechanism: Multi-faceted interventions that combine information, goal-setting, and social influence are effective in reducing energy consumption.
findings.quote: feedback in combination with other strategies such as goal setting [162] and peer education [163] could lead to between four and seven percent building energy reductions.

findings.consequent: Complex interplay between technologies, individuals' understanding/use of technologies, Influence on energy consumption
findings.mechanism: SPT highlights that energy consumption is embedded within social practices, which are shaped by the interaction of technologies, meanings, and competencies.
findings.quote: Social Practice Theory demonstrates the complex interplay between technologies and the ways in which individuals understand and use them as well as their influence on energy consumption

findings.consequent: Factors shaping occupants' outcomes (e.g., individual's choices) in terms of energy conservation behaviors
findings.mechanism: The framework provides a holistic view of how norms, practices, material culture, and external factors interact to shape energy-related behaviors.
findings.quote: perspectives from Energy Cultures have helped illustrate what factors shape occupants' outcomes... in terms of energy conservation behaviors.

findings.consequent: Cognitive norms, People's choice of technologies, Resulting impact on energy practices
findings.mechanism: The physical environment and available technologies influence mental models and behavioral routines related to energy use.
findings.quote: material cultures shape cognitive norms, people's choice of technologies, and the resulting impact on energy practices.

findings.consequent: Household behaviors (e.g., cooking practices), Reinforced by certain external factors
findings.mechanism: Social routines and external influences (e.g., pricing) shape daily household energy practices.
findings.quote: everyday social interactions determine household behaviors, such as cooking practices [114], reinforced by certain external factors [111,115].

findings.antecedent: Socio-cultural factors (even when controlling for building characteristics and household composition)
findings.mechanism: Cultural norms and social contexts play a dominant role in shaping heating behaviors, independent of physical building attributes.
findings.quote: socio-cultural factors significantly influence heating practices in residential buildings.

findings.antecedent: Interactions between different actors, Social networks (within and between households)
findings.consequent: Residents' low-carbon household behaviors, Energy efficiency performance (at inter-building level)
findings.mechanism: Social connections and collaborative actions can foster collective energy-saving behaviors and improve overall efficiency.
findings.quote: interactions between different actors and social networks embedded within and between households can significantly improve residents' low-carbon household behaviors and energy efficiency performance at the inter-building level

findings.antecedent: Demographic variables (gender, age, education, immigration status)
findings.mechanism: Individual demographic characteristics influence behavioral patterns related to energy use.
findings.quote: demographic variables on behavior in buildings... include gender and age [121,123], education, and immigration status [109].

findings.antecedent: Contextual factors (family scales, monthly incomes, consumption, housing size, living area, rehabilitation housing)
findings.mechanism: The socio-economic and physical context of a household influences its energy consumption patterns.
findings.quote: Contextual factors such as family scales, monthly incomes and consumption, housing size, living area [123], and rehabilitation housing [107] are also important factors in shaping energy use.

findings.consequent: Divergence of consumption patterns (between households living in similar conditions)
findings.mechanism: Established routines and habits can lead to different energy consumption outcomes even in similar physical environments.
findings.quote: vital role habits and broader behavioral routines play in explaining the divergence of consumption patterns observed between households living in similar conditions

findings.consequent: Ability to change ingrained habits over time
findings.mechanism: Deeply embedded cultural norms, personal motivations, and lack of long-term perspective make habit change difficult.
findings.quote: various factors (i.e., existing cultures, self-interest, short-sightedness, etc.) inhibit the ability to change ingrained habits over time

findings.consequent: Explaining how people do or do not change standby consumption habits
findings.mechanism: Standby consumption is often a routinized, unconscious behavior not solely driven by rational decision-making.
findings.quote: rational thought processes alone are not enough to explain how people do or do not change standby consumption habits.

findings.antecedent: Complex and intertwined nature of practices, material arrangements, infrastructures
findings.mechanism: Energy-related practices are deeply embedded in the socio-material context, making them difficult to change through conscious decisions alone.
findings.quote: heating and cooling practices stem in part from the complex and intertwined nature of practices, material arrangements, and infrastructures.

findings.antecedent: Framing information about energy use in terms of health consequences (vs. cost)
findings.mechanism: Framing effects can alter how individuals perceive the benefits of energy conservation, with health-related frames potentially leading to more sustained behavioral change.
findings.quote: framing information about energy use in terms of health consequences as opposed to cost produces more persistent reductions in energy use.

findings.antecedent: Beliefs of individuals regarding energy efficiency
findings.mechanism: A gap exists between self-perception of energy efficiency and actual behavior, suggesting that beliefs alone do not guarantee energy-saving actions.
findings.quote: inconsistencies between beliefs of individuals regarding energy efficiency and their actual actions, suggesting people who believe they are energy efficient often use as much energy as other households.

bridge_warrants: The paper's core function is to bridge various behavioral theories with occupant interactions in buildings, highlighting how different theoretical constructs explain specific behaviors across diverse building systems.
methodological_critiques: Limited empirical and naturalistic studies exist that attempt to explain occupant interactions with specific building systems through behavioral theories.
Many reviewed studies were conducted through surveys and questionnaires, which may not be sufficient to generalize how particular behavioral theories apply in these contexts.
There is a lack of proper design of studies, with some not including a control group or not reporting/measuring the influences of theoretical constructs.
Some studies were based on simulations that require further verification using real-world data.
The reliance on self-reported intentions to save energy versus actual (measured) savings leads to an 'Attitude-Behavior-Gap'.
There are trade-offs between sample size and feasibility of monitoring, but devices getting cheaper should alleviate this issue.
Many identified studies neglected the influence of environmental factors such as indoor/outdoor temperature or indoor air quality on window opening/closing behavior.
Studies need to be better designed by focusing on a specific behavioral theory, ensuring all constructs are explicitly considered and accounted for.
The relationship between experimental design and specific theories or constructs was not always clearly explained.
The lack of consistency in how theories have been applied makes it difficult to draw consistent conclusions about the most significant drivers of hot water use.
Relatively small sample sizes in some studies make it difficult to generalize findings across populations.
Many theories across all three disciplines (psychological, sociological, economic) are only applied once, making robust comparison difficult.
There is a disciplinary bias, with survey-based methods common for psychological theories and interview approaches for sociological theories.
The majority of studies were conducted in a select few countries (US, Western Europe, China), with very few in South America, Africa, Middle East, or Eastern Asia (excluding China).
limitations: The scope of the review is limited to the intentions and immediate actions of occupants that can be explained by behavioral theories, excluding physiological factors or feedback and intervention strategies that motivate occupants to reduce energy consumption.
The majority of identified studies applied very few and well-known theories (e.g., TPB, NAM, VBN), which may not always be the most appropriate for specific interactions.
The Theory of Planned Behavior and similar models have been criticized for oversimplifying behavior and being too linear for engineering models.
Many identified papers focused on applying only specific constructs within a theory, instead of considering all elements collectively.
There is a need for deeper dives into more nuanced behavioral theories beyond broad overarching theories.

The majority of studies were conducted in a select few countries and geographical locations (US, Western Europe, China), with very few in South America, Africa, Middle East, or Eastern Asia (excluding China).
There is no common agreement on the influence of the mentioned theories on mixed systems, likely due to differences in location, target sample, and number of analyzed buildings.
Results showed mixed effects of certain theories' constructs on energy-savings and energy conservation intentions, and mixed results regarding predictors of energy use.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control are key determinants of intentions, which in turn predict occupant energy-saving behaviors in buildings.
Personal values and ecological worldviews influence pro-environmental beliefs and personal norms, which are fundamental drivers of occupant energy-saving behaviors in buildings.
Self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and observational learning play crucial roles in shaping occupants' interactions with building systems and their energy-related behaviors.
Different goal frames (hedonic, gain, normative) activate distinct motivations that influence occupant decision-making and behavior regarding energy use in buildings.

mechanism_chain.description: A mechanism chain illustrating how psychological factors, as conceptualized by behavioral theories like the Theory of Planned Behavior, lead to energy-saving intentions and subsequent behaviors in a building context.
